# Changelog

## 0.42.0

Retired choices on value flags and positional args.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

A value flag or positional arg that declares choices may now also declare the spellings it used to accept, so a renamed value is refused with a message naming its replacement instead of the generic invalid-value error. The three implementations ship it together, each in its own declaration shape, with conformance cases covering every target.

</details>

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **Retired choices.** A value flag or positional arg that declares `choices` may also declare the spellings it used to accept, through `retiredChoices: [{ value: "old", message: "use 'new'" }]` on the flag and arg option objects. A value matching one is refused at parse time with the message naming its replacement, ahead of the invalid-value check and from every source the choices check already reaches. A retired value is not a choice: help never lists it, and the published `value_schema` enum and MCP tool schema carry the live set only. `--dump-schema` publishes the declaration as a `retired_choices` map.

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **The `effects-bypass` check reads only repository-owned files.** Its inputs are now what `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard` lists from the project root -- tracked files plus untracked files `.gitignore` does not exclude -- so a gitignored scratch file can no longer turn a release-blocking check red on one machine while a fresh clone is green. A project root outside a git work tree is refused (`effects-bypass: project root '<path>' is not a git work tree; the check reads only repository-owned files`), with no filesystem-walk fallback.
- [ts-strictcli] **A retired choice of the wrong type is refused at registration.** A `retiredChoices` entry whose value is not of the declaration's own type used to register as a dead declaration: the parse-time comparison is type-aware, so the spelling it named stayed accepted and its message never printed. It is now a registration-time error in the twin of the live choice type-mismatch sentence (`Flag "format": retired choice '8080' is not of type str`), on the flag and the arg surface alike.

## 0.41.0

Test coverage is anchored to a declared directory (test_coverage_dir, WithTestCoverageDir, testCoverageDir) instead of the current directory; the old boolean is refused. The package describes itself with the project's settled line.

### Breaking

- [ts-strictcli] **Breaking.** CLI test-coverage instrumentation is declared as a directory, not a boolean: `testCoverageDir: "<path>"` names the directory holding `coverage/` and `test-coverage.json`. The old `testCoverage: true` is refused at registration with an error naming the new option. An undeclared directory, or a declared one that does not exist at construction, leaves coverage off entirely -- so an installed CLI run from a consumer's project no longer registers the `cli-test-coverage` check there or reads and writes coverage state relative to whatever directory it was started in.

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **Fix.** The package description is now the project's canonical one-line description.

## 0.40.2

A plain CLI run no longer plants an empty .strictcli/coverage/ directory in the current directory, and the package describes itself with the project's canonical one-line description.

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] Enabling CLI test coverage no longer plants an empty `.strictcli/coverage/` directory in whatever directory you run the CLI from. The directory is now created only when a test actually records coverage.
- [ts-strictcli] **The project describes itself consistently everywhere.** The npm page now carries one canonical one-line description covering all three implementations, alongside a homepage, an issue-tracker link, and real discovery keywords.

## 0.40.1

A member-spelled choice's member flag can declare a short, closing the gap that made converting a group of flags into a member-spelled selector drop every short they had.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

The framework already promised this: §24.4 says a short declared on a member is an ordinary flag short, the refusal for a short on the selector itself says "declare the short on a member", and the short-claim table, the help renderer and the two sibling-scope short guards already read a member's short. Only Go could produce one. The short now goes on the declaration each member shape puts its electing flag on -- choice({value: {carrier, help, short}}) for a payload-carrying member, choice({help, short}) for a payload-less one -- and declaring it anywhere else is a compile error where the type system can see it and a registration error where it cannot.

</details>

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **A member-spelled choice's member flag can declare a short.** `choice({value: {carrier, help, short}})` declares a payload-carrying member's short and `choice({help, short})` a payload-less one's, so converting an at-most-one group of flags into a member-spelled selector no longer drops every short those flags had. The short elects at every door argv supports, renders beside its member in `--help`, publishes on the payload's schema entry, and is claimed against every simultaneously live scope.

## 0.40.0

The declaration-regime release: mandatory presence declarations, scoped selectors replacing mutex groups, real-JSON-Schema value fragments (schema v2), the co-occurrence constraint system, and the update-command construct.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

The declaration-regime campaign closes the last places where strictcli inferred something the developer had not written down: presence is now declared on every flag and arg, exactly-one selection is a scoped choice flag rather than a mutex group, `--dump-schema` publishes real JSON Schema value fragments at schema version 2, co-occurrence rules are one named constraint container, and an update command declares the resource, write mode, identity and properties it writes. Consumers must migrate their declarations before adopting this version: the new rules are registration-time hard errors, so an unmigrated app fails to build rather than misbehaving, and a repo that has not migrated simply stays on the previous floor until it does.

</details>

### Breaking

- [ts-strictcli] **Presence is now declared, never inferred.** `FlagOpts` is a discriminated union on `presence`: every flag declares exactly one of `{ presence: "required" }`, `{ presence: "optional" }` or `{ presence: "default", default: <value> }`, and `ArgOpts` moves onto the same union with `required?: boolean` deleted. Declaring none or two is a registration-time error, `default: null` is refused with a redirect to `presence: "optional"`, a list or dict flag no longer defaults silently to `[]` / `{}`, a variadic arg cannot declare a default, and a mutex member declares its own optionality instead of receiving a parse-time exemption. An optional flag or arg delivers `undefined` (bools become a real tri-state), and the inferred handler-args type follows the declaration -- which fixes the mutex-member key that was typed as always-present while the parser handed it `undefined`.
- [ts-strictcli] **Choices are a declaration scope.** `choiceFlag(name, choices, opts)` declares a flag whose type is its set of choices, each declared with `choice({ help, flags?, value? })` and owning the flags that exist only while it is elected. The handler receives one tagged value under the selector's own key -- a discriminated union derived from the literal choice map, so `switch (args.via.choice)` narrows and `assertNever` in the default branch is checked by the compiler, with no annotation written anywhere. Sub-flags are never top-level handler arguments at any depth, `provided(record, name)` answers provided-ness inside a scope, nesting is unlimited, and parsing is order-independent: `--subject hi --via email` parses exactly as `--via email --subject hi` does. A flag supplied outside its elected scope is its own parse error naming the flag, its owning choice and the choice that was elected -- never "unknown flag". A selector declares `required` or a `default` and never `optional`, a defaulted selection must be complete, and `choices` entries become `{ value, help? }` records with the bare-value spelling deleted -- `choices: ["a", "b"]` becomes `choices: [{ value: "a" }, { value: "b" }]`, and a flag whose entries carry help renders as an indented block instead of the one-line `[choices: a, b]` form.
- [ts-strictcli] **`mutexGroup` is removed.** Exactly-one-of-these is a member-spelled choice flag now: `memberChoiceFlag(name, choices, opts)` spells each choice as its own flag carrying its own payload, and it reproduces the mutex error sentences and the `--no-x` decline semantics byte-for-byte. There is no shim and no deprecation period -- replace `mutex: [mutexGroup({ a, b })]` with a `memberChoiceFlag` entry in the command's `flags` map. A member gains what a group could not express: a scope of its own, so `--profile work --create-missing` parses and `--all-profiles --create-missing` is a scope error, and a payload carried in the alternative that owns it, so the sentinel defaults on flags that meant nothing unless elected disappear. The handler receives one tagged record instead of one value per member, a member flag is `required once this member is elected` (inverting the rule that forbade requiredness on a member), and the `Flags (mutually exclusive):` help section is gone with the construct. Constraints now operate at root scope only: naming a scoped flag from `allOrNone`, `atLeastOne`, `requires` or `implies` is a registration error, because the scope already is the constraint.
- [ts-strictcli] **`--dump-schema` writes schema version 2.** A flag or arg entry carries a real JSON Schema fragment under `value_schema`, from a closed subset of `type`, `items`, `additionalProperties` and `enum` with JSON Schema's own type names; the `type` key and the `repeatable` key are gone, because arity is a property of the value and a variadic arg publishes the same array fragment a `list[T]` flag does. A value flag's `choices` splits in two: the values as an `enum` inside the fragment, and the value-plus-help records beside it under `choices` (`help` omitted when an entry declares none). A choice flag has no fragment at all -- its value is a variant the subset cannot express -- and instead publishes its nested choices and scopes, each scoped entry a full flag entry, with `elect_by` as the discriminator. Every entity's keys are emitted in a declared order, the document is written in one canonical encoding so two implementations' dumps are byte-comparable, and the `defaults` block is rewritten as the complete map of what an omitted key means. The dump also stops being blind to behavior: `config_format`, `config_path`, `config_conflict_mode`, per-flag `prefixed` and per-command `flag_sets` each appear exactly when a declaration departs from the framework's own behavior, `config_path` publishes the declaration rather than the machine's resolution of it, and the `checks` block is a function of the declaration alone.
- [ts-strictcli] **`provided()` over a caller-supplied elected record now answers `false` for every field.** The record door labels every field it delivers as the declaration's, so a handler can no longer tell a field the call supplied from one the declaration filled. The command line is unaffected and still answers what the invocation caused.
- [ts-strictcli] **Constraints, reshaped.** `coRequired` is deleted and `allOrNone` takes its place beside a new `atLeastOne`, both taking one option object with a mandatory `name` and passed through `constraints: [...]`. A member is a plain `{ name, when? }` record naming a flag, a positional arg or another named constraint, nested to unlimited depth; `members` is typed `[M, M, ...M[]]`, so a one-member constraint is a compile error, and `when` is the literal union `"present" | "true" | "non_empty"`, so a typo is one too. A bool member must declare its election, so `--no-x` can no longer engage a constraint while selecting nothing. `requires` and `implies` keep their semantics and take the same mandatory name. No member may declare `presence: "required"`. Constraints now render in `--help`, publish their members in `--dump-schema`, and project into MCP tool schemas as `anyOf` / `dependentRequired` with any remainder stated in the tool description.
- [ts-strictcli] **Three breaking changes, all of them the update-command round's.** (1) The mutating-default ban: a flag or positional arg on a command declaring `effect: "mutating"` may no longer declare a value default, because on a mutating command a value the framework picked is a value the framework writes -- empty collection defaults, `relativeToRoot()` defaults, a choice flag's own default and every declaration on a read_only command stay legal. (2) `config set` takes its value under `--value`: its write is now an exactly-one selection over a value, a clear and a reset to default (`config set <key> --value <v>`), and supplying none or two of the three is refused by the framework rather than by the command. (3) The machine envelope gains a `writes` member carrying an update command's write set, and `interface_version` becomes `2`.

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **`ctx.provided(name)`, and presence published everywhere it is asked about.** `ctx.provided` answers whether the invocation caused a flag's value -- true for `cli`, `env`, `config` and `implied`, false for `default` and `infra` -- so no handler reconstructs that boolean out of `ctx.source`. `--dump-schema` emits a `presence` key on every flag and arg entry plus a `default` exactly when presence is `"default"` (empty collections included), and the arg entry's `required` key is gone; help renders exactly one presence marker per line (`[required]`, `[optional]` or `[default: <value>]`), with required positionals and declared empty collections now visible; and MCP tool schemas read requiredness straight off the declaration, so a required bool finally appears in `required`.
- [ts-strictcli] **README explains the TypeScript-shaped declaration surface.** The package README now states that the TypeScript implementation is not a port of the Python or Go ones: flag and arg options are a discriminated union on `presence` (a `default` beside `presence: "required"` does not compile, and `presence: "default"` without a `default` does not either), the twin command factories narrow the handler's `ctx` so a `.write()` inside a read-only command is a compile error, and what the three implementations hold identical is behavior rather than spelling.
- [ts-strictcli] **The scope rule reaches the type system and the machine boundary.** A computed choice key is a compile error naming itself (it would silently degrade the delivered tag to `string` and make `assertNever` accept anything), a selector's `default` is typed `keyof C & string` so naming a choice that does not exist fails to compile before it fails to register, and a scoped sub-flag is unreachable as a top-level handler argument -- which is the structural fix for the handler-args unsoundness the mutex-member shape carried. Over MCP one command is still one tool: the selector contributes an `enum` property, every scoped flag contributes a top-level property that never appears in `required` (its requiredness is conditional), and the scope structure rides the tool description as a deterministic `Scoped parameters (enforced at call time):` block. A wrong combination is refused at call time with the same sentence the CLI parser gives.
- [ts-strictcli] **An integer `choices` entry beyond ±2^53 is refused at registration.** The dumped schema publishes a declaration's choices as a JSON Schema `enum`, and a reader that parses JSON numbers as IEEE-754 doubles -- which every reader of a schema file is entitled to be -- reads a different integer back. Declare a big identifier as a string instead. Float choices are unaffected: the canonical float form round-trips exactly, so nothing is lost there.
- [ts-strictcli] **A variadic positional arg accepts a list carrier.** `arg("files", t.list(t.str), { variadic: true, ... })` registers beside the element-carrier spelling `arg("files", t.str, { variadic: true, ... })`; both deliver the same array and publish the same schema fragment. The element spelling stays legal and stays the idiomatic one -- this widens the surface, it does not replace it. A list carrier on a non-variadic arg is still refused, and a dict carrier is refused on both.
- [ts-strictcli] **A choice name must match `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*`, checked at registration.** A choice name is a surface name whatever elects it -- a token-spelled choice flag publishes it in an enum, a member-spelled one puts it on the command line as a flag -- and TypeScript spells it as a property key of the choice map, which constrains nothing. `choice({...})` under a key like `Email`, `e_mail` or `1email` is now refused with `Flag "via": choice name "Email" must match [a-z][a-z0-9-]*` in both spellings, before member spelling's flag-name bans, so a name that fails both is reported as the charset failure it is.
- [ts-strictcli] **The README documents the choice flag.** A new section shows `choiceFlag`/`memberChoiceFlag` and `choice`, the derived discriminated union a `switch` narrows with `assertNever`, the compile-checked `default` typed `keyof C & string`, and the fact that `optional` has no union member at all; the feature list gains a choice-flag entry and drops the retired mutex one.
- [ts-strictcli] **The README documents the constraint system.** A Constraints section covers the four factories and their mandatory names, the `{ name, when? }` member object, the `members` tuple and `when` literal union that make a one-member constraint and a selector typo compile errors, the mandatory bool election, nesting with the help block it renders, the required-member refusal, and the root-scope rule.
- [ts-strictcli] **The update-command construct.** `updateOf: { resource, writeMode, identity, properties }` on a command spec declares what a command updates: which flags and args name the instance, which flags carry what changes, and whether the write is sparse or a full replace. `properties` is typed over the command's own declared names with a floor of one, so a property naming a flag the command does not declare -- and an empty list -- are compile errors. The framework enforces that at least one property is supplied, renders the write set on every surface a run reports through (one unnumbered line in the would-do log and a `writes` member on the machine envelope), and publishes the declaration in `--dump-schema` and in the MCP tool schema. A property declares `presence: "optional"`: absence means untouched, and `nullable: true` mints `--unset-<prop>`, answered by `ctx.unset(name)`.
- [ts-strictcli] **The package README documents the update-command construct.** A features entry covers `updateOf`, its `properties` tuple typed over the command's own declared names, the mutating-default ban, the at-least-one-property rule, the write set's two renderings and the minted `--unset-<prop>` spelling; the config entry carries `config set`'s reshaped `--value` argv.

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **A declared default never runs a flag's `validate` callback, and never counts as supplied.** A validator now sees only values the invocation caused -- CLI, env, config or an implication -- so a default the validator would reject no longer fails the parse when nothing is typed. The same one predicate decides presence for `allOrNone`, `requires` and `implies`, and it now excludes the `infra` source (a `relativeToRoot` default resolved through a declared root), which is the declaration deciding just as a plain default is.
- [ts-strictcli] **A structural parse problem is now reported ahead of a value that will not parse.** An unknown flag, an unknown choice and a scope violation are facts about the command line's shape, and shape is decided before any token's text is interpreted -- on every command, not only on one that declares a choice flag. `myapp cmd --count abc --unknown` reported `--count: expected integer, got 'abc'` and now reports `unknown flag '--unknown'`, and the answer no longer depends on which token came first.
- [ts-strictcli] **The MCP tool schema describes array parameters correctly.** A parameter whose value is a list carried its `enum` at the property root, which said the array itself had to equal one of the choices; it now sits inside `items`, describing an element. The projection derives its shape from the same arity rule the dumped `value_schema` fragment states, so a tool schema and a dumped schema cannot disagree.
- [ts-strictcli] **A positional arg with helped choices renders an indented block.** The block rule was always content-keyed -- any `choices` entry carrying help -- and it now reaches positional args exactly as it reaches flags: the entries render beneath the arg's line with their help, the one-line `[choices: a, b]` part is dropped in that form, and one alignment column is computed across the whole `Arguments:` section. A defaulted choice flag also renders its complete elected value (`[default: webhook (url=..., retries=5)]`) instead of the bare choice name, and a member-spelled choice flag's line carries its bare name with each member line ending in its own presence part.
- [ts-strictcli] **A member's payload property elects that member over MCP and `asTools`.** The flat machine form has no tokens, so supplying the property that flattens under a member's own flag name is that election: `{"profile": "work"}` now elects `--profile` and carries its value, exactly as `--profile work` does on the command line, without repeating the choice under the selector's own property. Supplying one member's payload beside a selector property naming a different member is a double election and is refused with the CLI's own sentence -- `--profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive` -- instead of a scope refusal that named the member's own election as the scope it was missing from. One level down the same rule holds: a payload key under an unelected outer scope names that outer scope, byte-for-byte as the parser does.
- [ts-strictcli] **A member name colliding with a command-level flag is reported as the duplicate flag name it is.** Electing a member IS the election, so a member's own name is a root token that opens no scope of its own. Declaring `memberChoiceFlag("mode", { profile: ... })` beside a command flag named `profile` -- or two member-spelled choice flags that both declare a `profile` member -- now raises `command "run": duplicate flag name "profile"` instead of the simultaneously-electable message, which could only state the collision with two empty scope paths. A member may still carry its own selector's name, which is never typed under member spelling, and a nested member colliding with a command-level flag keeps the scoped diagnosis.
- [ts-strictcli] **A refusal inside nested scopes names the outermost election that came from outside the command line.** A required sub-flag missing under two nested choice flags blamed the innermost election, so a scope elected from an environment variable beside a typed inner one said nothing at all about the variable that caused it. The clause now walks the scope path outermost first and names the first election that did not come from the command line -- `(elected from env var 'MYAPP_VISIBILITY')` -- and stays absent when every election on the path was typed.
- [ts-strictcli] **The flat machine form MCP and `asTools` take answers with the command line's own sentences.** Three refusals were wrong at that boundary. Elections ran one selector at a time, so an earlier selector's missing election was reported ahead of a later one's double election -- `{target: "all-profiles", profile: "work"}` on a command declaring a required `mode` first said `one of --fast, --slow is required` where the same command line says `--profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive`; every election now resolves command-wide, at every depth, before any scope, value or presence problem is reported. Electing a payload-carrying member through the selector's own key without its payload -- `{target: "profile"}` -- said `flag '--profile' is required under '--profile'`, naming the flag as its own owner, and is now `flag '--profile' requires a value`. And a payload-less member's own property was ignored, so `{all_profiles: true}` was refused with `one of --profile, --all-profiles is required` where `--all-profiles` elects; it now elects on `true` and declines on `false` exactly as `--no-all-profiles` does, decline clause and redundant-negation refusal included. A selector one level down also names the scope it sits in when it refuses, as it does on the command line.
- [ts-strictcli] **A record handed to `app.call()` electing a member with no `value` takes the same missing-value sentence.** `app.call("fetch", { source: { choice: "url" } })` reported `flag '--url' is required under '--url'`; a member flag is elected by its own token and that token carries the payload, so the refusal is now `flag '--url' requires a value` at both front doors.
- [ts-strictcli] **The machine boundary and `app.call()` answer with the command line's own sentences, in the command line's own order.** Four refusals were wrong. A key naming nothing the command declares was checked only after the selectors had been converted, so it lost to whatever that work found -- `{via: "email", nope: 1}` reported a missing election where the same command line reports `unknown flag '--nope'`; it is a fact about the object's shape and now outranks every election, scope, value and presence problem, at both doors, and a nested selector's own property is recognized so supplying one under a sibling scope is the out-of-scope refusal rather than an unknown-key one. `one of --profile, --all-profiles is required` put the decline note between the requirement and the scope it lives in and left out the clause naming the environment variable that elected that scope; the three clauses now compose as scope, then origin, then the decline note. A `relativeToRoot` default declared inside a choice's scope was delivered as the marker object itself where the same declaration at command level delivers the resolved path; it now resolves through the declared infrastructure root at every depth. And a pre-typed value is now checked against the type its declaration names -- at command level, inside a scope, on a member's payload and on an app-level global -- so `{count: "7"}` on an `int` flag is `--count: expected integer, got str` rather than a string handed to a handler, and `null` is a legal value for nothing: a flag that may be absent declares `presence: "optional"` and is delivered absent when the key is omitted.
- [ts-strictcli] **`app.call()` checks a positional arg's value, and stages its phases over the whole command.** A positional was stringified on the way in, so `{ count: "7" }` reached an `int` arg as the integer 7 and `{ name: 123 }` reached a `str` arg as `"123"`; an arg is a declaration exactly as a flag is, so the supplied value is now checked against the type it declares -- `argument 'count': expected integer, got str` -- every element of a variadic arg is checked on its own, and `null` is a legal value for nothing. The record door also walked one selector to its end before starting the next, so every stage below election was decided for one selector before the next selector's record was read: a value, a presence or a scope problem in the first record was reported ahead of a second selector's election refusal. Elections, record shapes, scopes, values and presence are now staged across the whole command at every depth, the lowest stage decides what is reported, and the value sweep runs in declaration order rather than the order the caller happened to write the object's keys.
- [ts-strictcli] **A required bool inside a scope names the tokens that satisfy it.** `flag '--verify' is required under '--via email'` left a reader looking for a value to type, where the same declaration at command level says `flag '--verify' must be passed as --verify or --no-verify`. The scoped form is now the root sentence plus the scope suffix -- and the origin clause after it, when an ambient election put the requirement there -- on the command line and at both programmatic front doors alike.
- [ts-strictcli] **A dash-spelled key is refused at `app.call()` too, and a wrong-typed value is heard before a missing election.** `call("run", { "dry-target": "x" })` was accepted and delivered where the same key at the flat machine form is `unknown parameter "dry-target" for command "run"`: a flag's dashed spelling is its command-line token, and both doors take the underscored parameter name the schema publishes. The pre-typed value check also ran downstream of the flat form's conversion, so `{ via: "email", retries: "nope" }` on a command with a second required selector reported the missing election instead of `--retries: expected integer, got str`; the check now runs in the value phase at both doors, ahead of presence and behind every shape, election and scope fact.
- [ts-strictcli] **A key an elected record's scope does not declare is refused, and a pre-typed positional binds to the arg its key names.** `call("run", { via: { choice: "email", retries: 1, bogus: 2 } })` recorded a scope violation spelling the key as a flag -- `flag '--bogus' is only valid under '--via email'` -- for a key naming nothing the command declares anywhere. A record's key namespace is the elected choice's own scope, so the answer is now `unknown parameter "bogus" for command "run" under '--via email'`, at every depth and carrying the whole scope path, reported ahead of every election, scope, value and presence problem in the same call; a flag a sibling scope declares is an unknown key inside a record too, while the same parameter at the flat form's top level keeps the out-of-scope sentence it already had. A scoped refusal two levels down also named only its innermost election, where the command line names the whole path. And positionals handed to `call()` were read densely in declaration order: on a command declaring an optional `label` before a required `count`, `call("run", { count: 2 })` bound 2 to `label` and answered `argument 'label': expected string, got int` -- a sentence about a key the caller never wrote. A value now binds to the arg its key names, and an omitted key is the absence presence answers.
- [ts-strictcli] **Two record-door refusals corrected.** An explicit `null` or `undefined` on an *optional* scoped field at `app.call()`'s record door now delivers absence -- a present field holding nothing -- instead of failing as a type error; that is how a caller writes an unset optional property, and required fields, defaulted fields and the flat door are all unchanged. And a `RelativeToRoot` naming an undeclared infra root inside a choice scope now says where it was declared (`... under '--via email' (elected by default)`) at every door instead of naming no scope at all.
- [ts-strictcli] **The command line's value phase now reports in the order the tokens were typed.** `myapp run --via email --retries nope --before nope` named the root flag (`--before`) whatever the order, because every root flag's value was resolved before any scoped one; both refusals are true, and the one printed is now the token that comes first. A scoped `validate` callback can no longer refuse ahead of a later token's coercion failure either -- every coercion failure is reported before any callback refusal, whatever the declaration order. `call()` and the flat machine form are unchanged: they sweep the command's declarations once, as they always have.
- [ts-strictcli] **A selection nobody elected now reports the declaration at the flat machine door.** A command whose selector declares a default was delivered through `asTools()` / MCP with `ctx.source('via')` answering `cli` and `ctx.provided('via')` answering true, even when the caller sent nothing at all -- where the command line and `call()`'s record form both answer `default` and false for the same declaration. All three doors now agree. A scoped flag supplied beside a defaulted election is still delivered, exactly as the command line delivers it.
- [ts-strictcli] **`config show` renders a `RelativeToRoot` default as the declaration.** The human table printed the marker object's internals -- its fields plus the source text of its `toString` -- instead of `db = RelativeToRoot('MYAPP_HOME', 'db.sqlite')  (source: default)`, which is what the other implementations print byte-for-byte. Under `--json` the payload carried the runtime's own casing; it now carries the machine-stable shape `--dump-schema` already uses, `{"relative_to_root": {"env_var": ..., "parts": [...]}}`. The resolved path is unchanged where it belongs: a run still delivers it, labelled `infra`.
- [ts-strictcli] **A refusal from a default-elected scope names what elected it at the flat machine door too.** A `RelativeToRoot` naming an undeclared infra root inside a selection nobody elected read `... under '--via email'` through `asTools()` / MCP, where the command line and `call()`'s record form both read `... under '--via email' (elected by default)` -- the clause exists to name the cause a reader cannot see in their own call, and a conversion is not a caller. Every scoped refusal at that door now carries it, at any depth, naming the outermost election no caller made. A caller's own election still earns no clause.
- [ts-strictcli] **A scoped value supplied at the flat machine door runs its `validate` callback.** A `validate` declared on a flag inside a choice's scope never ran for a value supplied through the flat machine form -- `tools/call` over `--mcp`, and a tool descriptor's `execute` -- so `{ via: "email", subject: "hi" }` was accepted where the same values typed as `--via email --subject hi` are refused with `--subject: hi is refused`. The callback is a property of a supplied value, and this door reads the caller's own keys, so it now runs for a scoped value exactly as it does for a root-scope one and for a typed token: at every depth, per element for a list, and never on a value the declaration decided. A coercion failure still outranks a validate refusal whatever the declaration order. `call()`'s record door is unchanged -- a constructed scope cannot tell a field the caller wrote from one it filled in, so it keeps the type check alone.
- [ts-strictcli] **A scoped value supplied at the flat machine door is checked against its `choices` list, and reports the call.** A closed set declared on a flag inside a choice's scope never constrained a value supplied through the flat machine form -- `tools/call` over `--mcp`, and a tool descriptor's `execute` -- so `{ via: "email", fmt: "xml" }` was accepted where `--via email --fmt xml` is refused with `--fmt: invalid value 'xml', must be one of: text, json`. A supplied scoped value now answers to the whole declaration there: the type, the closed set and the `validate` callback, with a coercion failure outranking both and an earlier field's callback outranking a later field's closed-set refusal. `provided()` over such a value now answers **true** with source `cli` too, as the command line answers for the same value -- that door reads the caller's own keys, so it no longer inherits the record door's uniform `default`. `call()`'s record door is unchanged.
- [ts-strictcli] **Registration reports the first error the contract pins when a constraint set has two faults.** The `Requires` / `Implies` operand guards ran early enough to outrank a required-member refusal, so an `Implies` whose trigger is not a bool was reported ahead of a co-occurrence member declaring `presence: "required"`. Those guards now run after every co-occurrence step, matching the Python and Go implementations.
- [ts-strictcli] **A constraint naming a member-spelled selector's election flag now says so.** `allOrNone`, `atLeastOne`, `requires` and `implies` reported `--all-profiles` as an unknown member or an unknown flag. The flag exists -- it is the token that opens its own scope -- so it now takes the scoped-operand refusal naming that scope, byte-identical to the sibling implementations.
- [ts-strictcli] **Registration reports the pinned first error when a constraint set has both a shape fault and an arity fault.** A bare-string member in a later constraint was reported only after an earlier constraint's "must declare at least two members" refusal. The member-record-shape check now runs across the whole set before any constraint's members are counted, so the bare name is named first -- matching the Python and Go implementations. Both faults are compile errors for a typed caller; the change is visible to a widened or JSON-shaped one.

## 0.39.0

Machine output becomes a framework-owned mode: reserved `--json`, one envelope as the sole stdout document, `ctx.payload()` against a `payloadSchema:` declaration replacing `outcome(exitCode, data)`, plus the process trace store, command-line-only mutex election, `ownsStdout`, and MCP protocol `2026-07-28` with consequential confirmation over both eras.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

Machine output used to be a per-command decision: a handler returned data
through `outcome(exitCode, data)` and the framework printed it, so every app
invented its own `--json` flag and its own document shape. This release makes
it a property of the framework. `--json` is reserved unconditionally at every
declaration level, recognised anywhere in argv with the same two boundaries as
the effects quartet, and delivered on the Context. Machine mode emits ONE
envelope as the sole stdout document -- payload, exit code, the dry-run preview
and every diagnostic the run emitted -- and `--quiet` cannot reach it. A
command's payload is a declared closed-subset JSON Schema, validated where the
envelope is written rather than at the `ctx.payload(...)` call, so a value the
envelope could not carry never fails a human-mode run. Payloads are plain
UTF-8, byte-identical with the Python and Go siblings.

Three further pieces ride the same release. The process trace store records
process ancestry at every real child-process start, chained through
`STRICTCLI_TRACE_PARENT` with a ULID identity and JSONL partitions, and stays
observational -- a forged ancestry identifier or an unwritable store leaves
stdout, stderr and the exit code byte-identical. Mutex election becomes
value-aware and command-line-only: a bool member elects only when it resolves
to true, so `--no-x` declines instead of choosing, and an env- or
config-sourced value neither elects a member nor reaches the handler.
`ownsStdout: true` plus claimed rendering let a command whose stdout IS the
artifact keep that stream clean while its diagnostics still reach the operator.

The MCP server moves to protocol `2026-07-28`: stateless, no handshake,
mandatory `server/discover`, per-request capabilities. A consequential
`tools/call` is no longer taken on the caller's word -- the server asks, over
the modern era's input-required `requestState` and over the retained
`2025-11-25` handshake's `elicitation/create`, from one mint-and-verify path.
The continuation is HMAC-protected, bound to the declared client and to a
digest of that exact request, single-use and five minutes long, and every exit
spends it, so a confirmation that was aborted cannot be re-answered later.

The breaking changes are a minor bump under pre-1.0 versioning. This is the
framework release the consumer projects' own releases depend on; the three
implementations ship the same behavior in lockstep, verified by the conformance
suite.

</details>

### Breaking

- [ts-strictcli] **Breaking.** `outcome(exitCode, data)` loses its data parameter, and the `check` and `config show` commands no longer declare a local `--json` flag. Handlers supply a machine payload through `ctx.payload(value)` on a command that declares `payloadSchema:`, and it is emitted only under the framework-owned `--json`; `test()` and `call()` still capture it. `config show` without flags now prints the human table instead of erroring, and `--plain --json` is legal.
- [ts-strictcli] **Breaking: a mutex group is now satisfied only by a command-line choice.** A bool member elects its group only when it resolves to true, so `--no-x` declines the option instead of choosing it; string members still elect on presence with any value, including `""`. Election is command-line-only: env and config values on a mutex member neither elect it nor reach the handler, and an unelected member delivers its declared default. A redundant negation beside a real election (`--profile work --no-all-profiles`) is now a parse error, and the unsatisfied-group error teaches: `one of --profile, --all-profiles is required (--no-all-profiles declines an option; it does not choose one)`. Hand-written "nothing was chosen" guards written against the old semantics are now dead code.
- [ts-strictcli] **Breaking: the confirmation refusals no longer print the flag that lifts them.** `error: stdin is not interactive; pass --approve-consequential to confirm` is now `error: stdin is not interactive; a consequential command must be confirmed at a terminal`, and `command '<path>' is consequential: pass approve_consequential to confirm` is now `command '<path>' is consequential: the call must carry confirmation`. Both consent mechanisms are unchanged and still documented -- a refusal is simply no longer where they are advertised. Any test pinning either text must be updated. Also breaking over MCP: a request that neither carries the current revision's `_meta` nor follows an `initialize` handshake is refused with `-32602` instead of being served.

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **New feature.** `--json` is a framework-owned flag reserved unconditionally at every level, recognised anywhere in argv, and delivered on the Context as `ctx.json`. Commands declare their machine payload's JSON Schema with `payloadSchema:`, published verbatim by `--dump-schema`.
- [ts-strictcli] **Machine mode emits one envelope.** `--json` now writes a single document carrying the payload, the exit code, the structured preview and every diagnostic the run emitted, instead of a bare payload line; human output is suppressed and `--quiet` cannot reach it. `app.effectLog()` joins the public App interface as the preview's source.
- [ts-strictcli] **Declared payload schemas are validated.** A command`s `payloadSchema:` literal is now checked at registration over a closed JSON Schema subset (`type` including type lists, `properties`, `required`, `items`, `enum`, `const`, `additionalProperties` as boolean-or-schema) -- an unknown keyword anywhere in it, typos included, is a hard error. At emission `ctx.payload(value)` validates the value against that declaration and refuses a deviation, naming the path into the value and the violated constraint, instead of shipping a wrong shape. The value is normalized through the machine-mode serializer first, so a BigInt is an integer token and a `Map` is an object, and every property test uses `Object.hasOwn`, so `__proto__` and `toString` are ordinary keys. Numbers are IEEE-754 doubles and any magnitude above 2^53 is refused, so a big identifier is a string by declaration. Optional builders (`schemaType`, `schemaArray`, `schemaObject`, `schemaEnum`, `schemaConst`) construct the same literal.
- [ts-strictcli] **Process ancestry is recorded universally.** At every real child-process start -- `ctx.effects.run`, `ctx.effects.spawn`, and an allowlisted observe, which really executes even in dry mode -- the framework mints a ULID, appends one JSON line describing the spawning invocation (app, version, command path, the reserved-flag state, machine mode, consent, effect classification, pid, and the parent identifier it inherited; never argv) to `~/.local/share/strictcli/trace/`, and composes `STRICTCLI_TRACE_PARENT=<that id>` into the child`s environment. A tool downstream reads the variable and resolves who invoked it from the store. Nothing in the framework reads the store back: there is no accessor, no code path branches on ancestry, and a forged identifier is a harmless false claim -- enforced by conformance sweeps asserting byte-identical output under a forged identifier and a broken store. Tracing is best-effort by design: a write failure never fails the run, never prints, is never retried, and leaves a write-once marker file. The full specification is `docs/process-trace-store.md`.
- [ts-strictcli] **New: `ownsStdout: true`.** A command whose stdout IS the artifact -- a SQL dump, an SVG, a hash-verified JSON document -- declares it, and in machine mode the envelope moves to stderr with its diagnostics so the artifact's bytes are untouched. Outside machine mode the declaration changes nothing, and `--dump-schema` publishes `owns_stdout` when it is declared.
- [ts-strictcli] **New: claimed rendering, `ctx.effects.recorded()` and `ctx.effects.renderLog()`.** A handler can now put the dry-run preview where it wants it instead of accepting the framework's end-of-dispatch position. Reading the records claims the render; `renderLog()` emits the identical bytes at the handler's chosen point; a claim that never rendered is still re-rendered at the seam, so a preview can never go missing.
- [ts-strictcli] **`--dump-schema` writes a declared location.** `createApp({ schemaPath })` takes a path or a `relativeToRoot(...)` marker; undeclared, the framework still writes `.strictcli/schema.json`, but anchored at the working directory the app was constructed in rather than wherever the process happens to stand when the flag is parsed.
- [ts-strictcli] **The MCP server speaks the current protocol revision (`2026-07-28`).** Every request declares its protocol version and the client's capabilities in `_meta`, and the block is validated down to the revision's key-name rules; `server/discover` replaces the handshake and advertises the supported versions, the capabilities and the server identity in one call; every result carries a `resultType`; the tool list carries its cacheability; and a version this server does not speak is refused with `-32022` naming what it does. The `initialize` handshake still answers and selects the older era for that process, so a handshake-era client keeps working.
- [ts-strictcli] **A consequential tool now asks before it runs.** Over the current protocol revision, an MCP `tools/call` on a `consequential` command from a client that declares elicitation support is answered with a confirmation request rather than a refusal; the client puts the question to a human, and the retry carrying the acceptance runs the command. Decline, cancel and an acceptance that says no all abort. The state the client echoes back is integrity-protected, bound to that client and that exact request, expires in five minutes and cannot be redeemed twice. The server declares the feature by name -- `dev.smmh.strictcli/consequential-confirmation` -- in `server/discover`.
- [ts-strictcli] **A consequential tool now asks the handshake era too, and tells a client that cannot be asked what it lacks.** Over the current revision, an unconsented consequential `tools/call` from a client whose `_meta` capabilities do not cover a form elicitation is answered `-32021` with `data.requiredCapabilities` instead of being refused as tool content. The retained `initialize` handshake now answers `2025-11-25`, the newest handshake-based revision, and confirms the way that era does: a server-initiated `elicitation/create` request whose JSON-RPC id is the same integrity-protected continuation the modern era puts in `requestState`, verified on return through the same path. There, anything but an explicit acceptance aborts, and a legacy client that declared no elicitation still gets the consent seam's refusal. The handshake also declares the feature by name under `capabilities.experimental`.

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **One broken check no longer aborts the whole check run.** A check implementation that throws is contained and reported as that check's own failure, naming the check, the thrown value's type and its message; every other check still runs and the run still fails.
- [ts-strictcli] **`check --dry-run` now runs the checks declared pure and lists only the rest.** The dry-run surface and the purity partition disagreed: one printed a plan and ran nothing, the other executed the pure checks. A dry run now executes the read-only checks it always claimed to preview, renders the impure remainder as the would-run plan, and exits nonzero when a pure check really fails.
- [ts-strictcli] **Fix.** `check --json` and `config show --json` no longer print nothing under `--quiet`: machine output is structurally exempt from quiet, as it already was on the Python and Go implementations.
- [ts-strictcli] **Fixed: the `check` command branched on `--json` to decide whether to supply a payload.** It now supplies it unconditionally, so the listing and results text ride the envelope's `diagnostics` in machine mode exactly as the Python and Go implementations emit them.
- [ts-strictcli] **Fixed: the process trace store's documented lookup rule.** A consumer that resolved an entry with one binary search over the partition filenames could report a live entry as a dangling parent -- the rolling rule strands entries above their own file's label. The specification now states the range invariant as one-sided (the clamp bounds the bottom only) and requires a backward walk through older partitions when the search misses. Writers are unchanged.
- [ts-strictcli] **Fixed: a payload is validated against its declared schema at emission, not when `ctx.payload(...)` is called.** A handler that supplies a value the envelope cannot carry -- a number above 2^53, for instance -- no longer fails a run that was never going to emit one; `--json` still refuses it with the same message. The reported case was `config show` against a config file holding a float above 2^53, where the human `--plain` path hard-errored; that command now builds and supplies its payload unconditionally in both modes.
- [ts-strictcli] **A consequential command could run after its confirmation was aborted.** In the handshake era (`2025-11-25`), a confirmation exchange that ended without a well-formed answer -- the connection closing, a JSON-RPC error response, or a reply under an id the server never sent -- left its single-use continuation unspent. The same client could then present that blob as the modern era's `requestState`, with an acceptance it wrote itself, and the consequential command it had just aborted ran. Every exit now spends the continuation, so an aborted question cannot be re-answered.
- [ts-strictcli] **A `requestState` is now refused unless it is spelled in canonical unpadded base64url.** A blob carrying one `=` of padding, or any character outside the alphabet, was accepted here and refused by the Go implementation, which ran the consequential command; a final character whose ignored trailing bits are non-zero was accepted by all three. Both segments are validated before decoding, identically in every implementation.
- [ts-strictcli] **A request whose `_meta` carries more than one offending key now names the same key in every implementation.** The key set is validated in sorted order -- over UTF-8 bytes, not UTF-16 code units -- so the refusal is the lexically first offender rather than whichever bad key the document happened to list first.

## 0.38.0

Consequential commands now require explicit consent on the programmatic and MCP channels, tool descriptors publish their effects classification, and `approve_consequential` becomes a reserved parameter name.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

The confirmation requirement was a CLI-only property: a command marked
`consequential` prompted (or refused) when it was reached through argv, but the
same command was reachable with no consent at all through `asTools()`,
`call()`, `Tool.execute` and MCP `tools/call`. An agent driving the app over
MCP therefore ran exactly the commands the requirement exists to stop for a
human decision. This release makes consent a property of the command rather
than of the channel: every call path refuses a `consequential` command unless
the caller states consent through the new `CallOptions` argument, and the
descriptors published to tool and MCP consumers carry `effect` and
`consequential` so a caller can see the requirement before it calls.

Reserving `approve_consequential` follows from that: the name is now framework
vocabulary in all three implementations, so no command may redefine it.

Both changes are breaking, which under pre-1.0 versioning is a minor bump. The
three implementations ship the same behavior in lockstep, verified by the
conformance suite.

</details>

### Breaking

- [ts-strictcli] **Tool export and programmatic calls honour the confirmation requirement.** `asTools()` descriptors and MCP `tools/list` now publish `effect` and `consequential` beside the argument schema, so a caller can see which tools require confirmation. `call()`, `Tool.execute` and MCP `tools/call` refuse a `consequential` command unless the call states consent (the new `CallOptions` argument's `approveConsequential`, or the `approve_consequential` param on an MCP `tools/call`).
- [ts-strictcli] **`approve_consequential` is a reserved parameter name.** `flag("approve_consequential", ...)` and `arg("approve_consequential", ...)` now throw at registration. The name is how a caller states consent to a `consequential` command (`CallOptions.approveConsequential`, or the `approve_consequential` param on an MCP `tools/call`), so it is framework vocabulary in every implementation and no command may redefine it.

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] The built-in `config` subcommands (path, show, set, edit, init) now explain what they actually do — precedence order, type coercion, comma-escaping and dry-run behavior — instead of one terse line.

## 0.37.0

Receiver-aware `effects-bypass` lint: `RegExp.prototype.exec` is no longer a false positive.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

The `effects-bypass` check matched the bare leaf name `exec`, so `pattern.exec(line)`
in a handler was reported as an escaped effect. The leaf is now a finding only bare
or through a child_process receiver (`cp`, `childProcess`, `child_process`, `execa`,
`shelljs`), matching the receiver-aware resolution on the Python side.

Consumers pick the fix up on their next lock bump.

</details>

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **`effects-bypass` no longer flags `RegExp.prototype.exec`.** The `exec` leaf is a finding bare or through a child_process receiver (`cp`, `childProcess`, `child_process`, `execa`, `shelljs`); `pattern.exec(line)` in a handler is no longer reported.

## 0.36.0

Adds the `dryRunSupported: false` command declaration -- a mutating command can now refuse `--dry-run` with a mandatory reason carried into help and the schema -- generates the exported `VERSION` constant from package.json so it can no longer report a version the package never shipped, and rewrites an npm README usage example that did not compile.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

`--dry-run` is a promise: the preview must describe what the real run would do.
Some mutating commands cannot keep that promise, because their effects are not
representable ahead of time. Until now such a command either rendered a preview
that misrepresented it or hand-rolled a refusal inside the handler -- after
parsing, invisible to `--help` and to `--dump-schema`. `dryRunSupported` moves the
refusal to the registration site on both twin factories and both passthrough
twins, where the framework can enforce it: the reason is mandatory, it is rendered
in a dedicated `Dry run:` help section, it is emitted in the schema, and declaring
it on a `read_only` command throws at registration (a command that changes nothing
has nothing to preview).

`VERSION` was a hand-written literal with a test pinning that literal, so the test
protected the drift instead of catching it. It is now generated from package.json
by the prebuild hook that `prepack` inherits, and the test asserts agreement with
the manifest rather than a constant.

The same release completes a documentation truth pass. Every registration example
was re-checked against the shipped API, and the reserved flag quartet, the effects
regime and the `consequential` confirm protocol are now documented. Examples are
no longer trusted by inspection: the self-contained example programs are marked
`validate`, and `selfdoc check` now type-checks and RUNS each one against the
built `dist`, so documentation that stops working fails the release.

</details>

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **`dryRunSupported: false` command declaration.** A mutating command whose effects a preview cannot honestly represent can now declare `dryRunSupported: false` with a mandatory `dryRunUnsupportedReason` on the twin factories and the passthrough twins. `--dry-run` is then refused at parse time with the reason instead of rendering a preview that would misrepresent the real run; the reason also appears in a new `Dry run:` help section and in the schema. Declaring it on a `read_only` command throws at registration time.

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **`VERSION` no longer lies.** The exported `VERSION` constant is now generated from `package.json` at build time, so it always matches the published package version -- it previously reported `0.31.0` in packages published as 0.35.0.
- [ts-strictcli] **The npm README's usage example now compiles.** It imported and called a `command()` factory that was removed when classification became mandatory, passed flags as an array instead of a keyed map, used a nonexistent `required: true` flag option, called `createApp` with a positional name and a `commands` key that `AppSpec` has never had, and declared a flag named `dry-run` -- a framework-reserved name that throws at registration. The example is now a working `createApp` + `defineMutatingCommand` program, and the feature list documents the twin factories, the effects regime, `dryRunSupported` and the confirm protocol.

## 0.35.0

Confirmation keys on a declared `consequential`, not on `mutating`

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

The shipped regime INFERRED "mutating => must confirm". Adoption across six
consumers falsified that inference by an order of magnitude: 391 of 624
commands (63%) classify `mutating`, against roughly 5-10% that are genuinely
dangerous -- a ~1:10 signal-to-noise ratio that guarantees the skip flag gets
passed reflexively and leaves the guardrail dead while it still looks present.

One field was answering two questions. `effect` correctly answers "should a dry
run record rather than execute?" -- unchanged. Consequence asks "are these
effects worth interrupting someone for?", which almost nothing answers yes to.
Commands now declare it with `consequential: true` on the twin-factory options
object, and the declaration is named after a property of the COMMAND rather
than after the framework's reaction so other behaviours can hang off the same
fact later.

</details>

### Breaking

- [ts-strictcli] **Confirmation now keys on a declared `consequential`, not on `mutating`.** Commands opt in with `consequential: true` on the twin-factory options object; a plain `mutating` command never prompts. The skip flag is `--approve-consequential` (`--yes` is gone, and the name `yes` stays banned for command and global flags); `ctx.yes` becomes `ctx.approveConsequential`. `consequential: true` on a `read_only` command or passthrough throws at registration, and the new `consequential-grant-agreement` check warns when a command declares a process- or network-mutating grant without declaring itself consequential.

## 0.34.2

Dry-run previews render on every exit path out of a handler

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

A consumer migrating onto the effects regime found that a dry-run preview vanished whenever the handler left through anything other than a normal return. The would-do log was rendered only on the success path, so a handler that recorded its intended writes and then exited non-zero -- the ordinary shape of a validation command -- printed nothing at all. Safety was never at risk (dry mode still executed nothing), but the preview property was: silence is indistinguishable from 'this command would do nothing', and those runs are exactly the ones a reader most wants to see. The render is now owned by the single seam every dispatch already passes through in each language, so it cannot be missed by a path that forgets to call it. An unexpected crash still renders what was recorded, followed by a new stderr marker saying the preview may be incomplete; the exception itself is never swallowed. A handler that terminates the process itself (Go os.Exit, Node process.exit) remains outside the guarantee and is recorded as a ceiling in the effects contract.

</details>

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **Dry-run previews no longer vanish on a crash.** A `mutating` handler that recorded effects and then threw printed nothing at all under `--dry-run`; the would-do log now renders on every exit path the framework can reach, and a thrown error marks the preview as possibly incomplete on stderr before rethrowing.

## 0.34.1

Recognize the reserved flag quartet anywhere in argv

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

The quartet (--dry-run, --yes, --quiet, --verbose) was extracted by a pre-scan
that stopped at the first non-flag token, so it was only recognized BEFORE the
command name -- while every documented invocation in this ecosystem writes these
flags after it. `myapp deploy --dry-run` failed with `unknown flag '--dry-run'`,
and the first consumer to migrate onto the effects regime had to rewrite argv
before handing it to the framework to make its own documented commands work.

The quartet is now recognized anywhere in argv, matching the framework's own
existing precedent for --help/-h. Two boundaries are preserved: a bare `--`
(everything after it is positional data) and a passthrough command's name (its
args belong to the child process and are forwarded byte-for-byte, so a child's
own --verbose is never eaten). --hermetic, --config, --dump-schema and --mcp
stay pre-command-only. Effects contract §7.2 is amended accordingly (adoption
ruling A1, §18.6).

</details>

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **The reserved flags now work after the command name.** `--dry-run`, `--yes`, `--quiet` and `--verbose` are recognized anywhere in argv, exactly like `--help` -- `myapp deploy --dry-run` used to fail with `unknown flag` and now works, at any group nesting depth. A bare `--` still ends recognition, and a passthrough command's args are still forwarded to the child untouched.

## 0.34.0

The effects regime: twin registration factories replacing defineCommand, framework-owned --dry-run/--yes/--quiet/--verbose, and side effects that flow through ctx.effects.

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

A consumer command once accepted a dry-run flag, ignored it, and published to a
public registry for real. Honoring a dry run was a convention, and conventions
are forgettable. This release makes it structural, in lockstep with the Python
and Go implementations.

Classification is mandatory and has no default, so there is nothing left for
defineCommand to mean: it is removed, along with passthrough, in favour of the
twins defineReadOnlyCommand / defineMutatingCommand and readOnlyPassthrough /
mutatingPassthrough. The twins pay for themselves at compile time -- a read-only
command's ctx is narrowed to a context that has no mutating methods, so a stray
.write() inside one is a type error, not a runtime surprise. Plain JavaScript
consumers get the same guarantee at runtime through a mandatory seal. The
framework owns --dry-run, --yes, --quiet and --verbose, and declaring a flag by
one of those names is a registration error.

Side effects ride ctx.effects: run, spawn, write, mkdir, remove, rename, chmod,
http. In a dry run the handle records instead of performing and prints the
would-do log. What a recorded mutation returns is the hard part, and the answer
is to refuse to guess: the handle returns a branded Unsettled carrier. Forward
it into a later effect and the preview continues with the provenance rendered
inline; read it or branch on it and the preview truncates with a message naming
the step and the reason.

One packaging change comes with this: the built-in effects-bypass check analyses
consumer sources through the TypeScript compiler API, so typescript moves from
devDependencies to dependencies and is installed alongside strictcli in
production installs. That was a deliberate trade -- full AST fidelity in
lockstep with the Python and Go checks was worth a dependency that most
consumers of a TypeScript CLI framework already have.

This breaks every consumer at its lock bump, deliberately: a silent grace period
would have preserved the exact bug class this regime exists to kill. The fleet
migrates in a dedicated wave immediately after this release.

</details>

### Breaking

- [ts-strictcli] **Breaking: the effects regime.** Every command must now be registered through the twin factories `defineReadOnlyCommand` / `defineMutatingCommand` (and passthroughs through `readOnlyPassthrough` / `mutatingPassthrough`) — `defineCommand` and `passthrough` are removed, because classification is mandatory and has no default. `--dry-run`, `--yes`, `--quiet` and `--verbose` are reserved framework flag names, delivered on the Context (`ctx.dryRun`, `ctx.yes`, `ctx.quiet`, `ctx.verbose`) and gating `ctx.info`/`ctx.debug`. `ctx.effects` mints the eight recorded operations (`run`, `spawn`, `write`, `mkdir`, `remove`, `rename`, `chmod`, `http`); under `--dry-run` they are recorded, not executed, and rendered as a would-do log, with `Unsettled` carriers that forward into later effects and truncate honestly when extracted from. A read-only command's handler `ctx` is narrowed so a `.write()` inside one is a compile error. Mutating commands prompt for confirmation unless `--yes` is passed. A built-in `effects-bypass` check fails on direct process, filesystem or network calls inside effects-using handlers.

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **`typescript` is now a runtime dependency.** The built-in `effects-bypass` check analyses consumer sources with the TypeScript compiler API, so `typescript` moved from `devDependencies` to `dependencies` and is installed alongside `strictcli` in production installs.
- [ts-strictcli] **New built-in `observe-allowlist-breadth` check (severity `warn`).** A single-token `procObserveAllowlist` prefix such as `["git"]` exempts an entire binary: every matching invocation executes for real under `--dry-run`, is never logged, and is legal inside a `read_only` command. The check names each one; `--ignore-warnings` clears it.

### Fixes

- [ts-strictcli] **`config set`, `config init` and `config edit` now honour `--dry-run`.** The framework's own mutating commands routed their writes (and `config edit`'s `$EDITOR` launch) around `ctx.effects`, so a dry run printed "no changes were made" while rewriting your config file and opening your editor. Every mutation now rides the handle and is recorded, not performed.
- [ts-strictcli] **Two effects-regime correctness fixes.** (1) The dry-run preview no longer skips numbers: framework-blessed cache writes (the schema dump and test-coverage shards) consumed would-do sequence numbers they never rendered, so a coverage-instrumented dry run began its preview at `2.` and every `«step N output»` brand and truncation "ends at step N" shifted with it — cache writes now carry their own counter. (2) `ctx.effects.run`'s `check` and `stream` and `ctx.effects.http`'s `check` now reject a forwarded carrier instead of silently ignoring it in dry mode.
- [ts-strictcli] **The confirm prompt accepts a CRLF-terminated answer.** A `y` typed at a console whose terminal ends lines with CRLF was read as `y\r` and declined. The answer's line terminator is now stripped as exactly one newline then exactly one carriage return; `  y` still declines.
- [ts-strictcli] **The `effects-bypass` check now analyses everything reachable from a registered command handler.** It previously only looked inside brace blocks that mentioned `ctx.effects`, so two shapes escaped completely: a handler that never mentions the handle, and a bypass one helper-call away. Roots are now `handler:` properties (inline or naming a declared function) plus, as before, any scope that uses the handle, and the check follows an intra-file call graph transitively. `typescript@7` ships no in-process parser, so reachability stops at the file boundary — that limit is documented rather than implied. Expect this check to surface findings it previously missed.

## 0.33.0

Add isHermetic() to the check-side ConnectionEnvReader

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **Hermetic detection in checks.** `ConnectionEnvReader` now exposes `isHermetic()`, letting a check distinguish `--hermetic` suppression from an unset connection env (both surface as `connectionEnvValue` present=false) and honor hermetic even when the env is absent.

## 0.32.0

Connection env vars: a hermetic-suppressed, app-level env primitive for connection URLs

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

Adds a third infra-env kind alongside infra roots and handshake vars. A connection env (e.g. a database DSN) is declared once at app level via createApp connectionEnv, read lazily with no default, and suppressed under --hermetic so connection-dependent behavior (including checks) skips visibly. Flags bind to it via connectionUrl/connectionEnv and check functions can read it through the ConnectionEnvReader capability.

</details>

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **Connection env vars.** Declare a hermetic-suppressed connection URL (e.g. a database DSN) at app level with `createApp({ connectionEnv })`; bind flags to it with `connectionUrl`/`connectionEnv`, read it from handlers via `ctx.connectionEnvValue()`, and from checks via the `ConnectionEnvReader` capability. Under `--hermetic` it resolves absent so connection-dependent behavior skips visibly.

## 0.31.0

Native TypeScript implementation

<details>
<summary>Context</summary>

Versions <=0.30.1 were an npm wrapper that installed the Python package via pip. From 0.31.0, strictcli on npm is a native TypeScript implementation. Python users: install strictcli from PyPI instead. This version begins the TypeScript era of the strictcli npm package.

</details>

### Features

- [ts-strictcli] **Native TypeScript implementation.** strictcli on npm is now a native TypeScript implementation (ESM, Node >= 22) with full static handler-arg inference from flag declarations, behavioral byte-parity with the sibling implementations enforced by the cross-language conformance suite.
